name: Modern C++ Programming Cookbook 3rd ed.: parallel map and fold with std::thread
workload: Chapter08/recipe_8_09.h test_mapreduce_threads: in-place map (i+i) and fold (sum into long long) over a std::vector<int> of 10,000 to 50,000,000 elements, one thread per hardware thread, timed with a microsecond chrono perf_timer, single run per size.
claimed_speedup: Book-reported at 50,000,000 ints: map 27457 us parallel vs 60049 us sequential (about 2.2x, derived from the book figures), fold 19075 us vs 41374 us (about 2.2x, derived). Parallel is faster only above roughly 2 million elements; below that the thread start-up cost loses.
hardware: Windows 64-bit, Intel Core i7 with 4 physical and 8 logical cores (per the book; exact model not stated)
tradeoffs: Hand-rolled chunking: splits the range into hardware_concurrency() equal parts, one std::thread each, no thread pool, no exception propagation (an exception in a worker calls std::terminate), threshold of 10,000 elements below which it falls back to the sequential algorithm. parallel_fold needs an associative operator and starts each partial sum from R{}. Needs random-access iterators. Up to hardware_concurrency extra threads per call.
caveats: The timing numbers are the book's own (quoted in the seed lead); the repository carries the benchmark program but no results file, so the numbers do not appear on the benchmark_url page and the ratios could not be checked against it. First-party book measurement, tier C: one run per size (the book itself notes run-to-run variation), compiler, optimisation flags and exact CPU not stated for this recipe; the repository's top-level CMakeLists adds only '/EHc /std:c++latest' for MSVC and '-std=c++2a -fexceptions -g -Wall' for GCC and Clang, so GCC and Clang builds through that file carry no optimisation flag. The baseline is single-threaded, so the gain is thread count (8 logical on 4 cores) and not a better algorithm; both loops are probably memory-bound, which would cap the gain well below the thread count. The sequential fold figure differs between this recipe (41374 us) and the std::async recipe (58689 us) for the same 50M elements, a spread as large as some of the claimed gains. Technique is an idiom, not a library: std::reduce or std::transform with std::execution::par (recipe 8.11) does the same job.

name: Modern C++ Programming Cookbook 3rd ed.: parallel map and fold with std::async tasks
baseline: Sequential std::transform and std::accumulate (the std::thread version is a second reference)
workload: Chapter08/recipe_8_10.h test_mapfold_tasks: in-place map (i+i) and fold (sum into long long) over a std::vector<int>; version1 launches hardware_concurrency std::async(std::launch::async) tasks over equal chunks; version2 is a recursive halving variant; microsecond chrono perf_timer, single run per size.
claimed_speedup: Book-reported at 50,000,000 ints: version1 map 22216 us vs 59665 us sequential (about 2.7x, derived from the book figures), fold 12942 us vs 58689 us (about 4.5x, derived); faster than the std::thread version, especially for fold. The recursive version2 (map half deferred) was no better than sequential.
hardware: Windows 64-bit, Intel Core i7 (assumed the same 4 physical, 8 logical core machine as the std::thread recipe; not restated)
tradeoffs: Same chunking scheme as the std::thread recipe but with std::async futures, so worker exceptions propagate through future::get in the fold (the map waits with wait(), which does not rethrow). std::launch::async spawns a thread per task (implementation may or may not pool them); no pool control, threshold of 10,000 elements for the sequential fallback.
caveats: The timing numbers are the book's own (quoted in the seed lead); the repository carries the benchmark program but no results file, so the numbers do not appear on the benchmark_url page and the ratios could not be checked against it. The shipped test in recipe_8_10.h stops at 10,000,000 elements (sizes 10000 to 10000000), so the 50,000,000-element row the book quotes cannot be produced without editing the size list. First-party tier C: single run per size, compiler, flags and CPU model not stated. The sequential fold baseline is 58689 us here against 41374 us in the std::thread recipe for the same data size, so the fold ratio (about 4.5x) is probably inflated by a slow or noisy baseline run; map baselines agree within 1% (59665 vs 60049 us). The baseline is single-threaded, so the gain comes from 8 threads and not a better algorithm. version2 uses std::launch::deferred for the map half, which runs on the calling thread, so it is effectively sequential and a poor foil.

name: Qt 6 C++ GUI Programming Cookbook 3rd ed.: raw heap array instead of std::vector and QVector
baseline: std::vector<int> filled with push_back (no reserve) and summed with at()
workload: Chapter14/Optimizing/main.cpp: fill 100,000,000 ints (0..N-1) then sum them, with new int[] and index access, std::vector push_back plus at(), and QVector push_back plus at(); one QElapsedTimer run each, printed with qDebug before the Qt event loop starts.
claimed_speedup: Book-reported: raw array 650 ms, std::vector about 3,830 ms (about 5.9x slower than the array, derived from the book figures), QVector about 5,400 ms (about 8.3x slower, derived).
tradeoffs: A plain new[] array has a fixed, known size, no growth, no bounds checking and no RAII (a leak or double delete is the caller's problem); std::vector or std::unique_ptr<int[]> keeps the safety. The win only applies when the element count is known up front.
caveats: The timing numbers are the book's own (quoted in the seed lead); the repository carries the benchmark program but no results file, so the numbers do not appear on the benchmark_url page and the ratios could not be checked against it. Idiom difference more than a container difference: the array is allocated once at full size and indexed with operator[], while the vector grows by push_back with no reserve() (repeated reallocation and copying of up to 400 MB) and is read through bounds-checked at(); a reserved vector read with operator[] would close most of the gap. Compiler, flags and CPU are not stated; the .pro file sets no optimisation flags and Qt Creator's default build configuration for a new project is usually Debug, in which case std::vector and QVector overhead (no inlining) is exaggerated. Each test runs once, in a fixed order (array first), and the returned sums are unused. The code sits in an application main() beside a GUI start-up, not a standalone benchmark.

name: The Art of Writing Efficient Programs: branchless destination selection by pointer-array indexing
baseline: if/else accumulate loop with an unpredictable (random 0/1) condition, as compiled by the same compiler
workload: Chapter03/02_branch.C BM_branched against BM_branchless (Google Benchmark): N random unsigned longs and a random 0/1 int condition array; each element is added to one of two sums, by if/else versus a[b1[i]] += p1[i] with a two-pointer array.
claimed_speedup: Book: the branchless loop is about 3.5 times faster than the loop with the unpredictable branch (text figure; the chart itself is an image).
compiler_and_flags: Clang 11 on x86 per the book chapter text; no flags stated for this file (the Chapter02 ReadMe suggests -g -O3 --std=c++17 for the Chapter02 programs only)
tradeoffs: Only pays when the condition is unpredictable: the same chapter shows a well-predicted branch beats the indexed form. The indexed store through an array of two pointers can defeat vectorisation and costs readability.
caveats: The timing numbers are the book's own (quoted in the seed lead); the repository carries the benchmark program but no results file, so the numbers do not appear on the benchmark_url page and the ratios could not be checked against it. The BENCHMARK(...) registration lines in 02_branch.C are all commented out, so the reader must uncomment BM_branched and BM_branchless to rerun it. The ratio is compiler-dependent: a modern -O2/-O3 compiler may already turn the baseline if/else into conditional moves or the indexed form into something else, and Clang 11 is old. Data are rand() & 1 over a vector sized by the benchmark argument (not stated in the text). Same chapter covers a related two-expression branchless case without a numeric ratio (see the no-evidence file).

name: The Art of Writing Efficient Programs: contiguous std::vector instead of std::list for sequential traversal
workload: Chapter04/03_list_vector.C (Google Benchmark): sequential iterator read and write of 1,048,576 unsigned long elements in std::vector versus std::list, 32x unrolled loop with DoNotOptimize on each access.
claimed_speedup: Book: list access just over 5 ns per value versus about 0.6 ns per value for the vector, almost an order of magnitude (about 8x, derived from the book figures); footprint 8 MB versus 24 MB.
hardware: x86; CPU model not stated, caches 32 KB L1, 256 KB L2, 8 MB L3 per the book
tradeoffs: Vector loses O(1) middle insert and erase and pointer stability on growth; the 3x memory footprint of the list (node headers) is part of the gain.
caveats: The timing numbers are the book's own (quoted in the seed lead); the repository carries the benchmark program but no results file, so the numbers do not appear on the benchmark_url page and the ratios could not be checked against it. Library and compiler not stated, so the result is for one unnamed standard library. The list is built by consecutive allocations in a fresh process, so its nodes are probably laid out nearly in order; a fragmented list from a long-running program would be slower. Well-known result, so this is an example of the idiom rather than new evidence; the file also defines but does not register the __m128i and __m256i vector variants.

name: The Art of Writing Efficient Programs: signed int loop index in substring comparison
baseline: std::sort with a hand-written substring comparison that uses an unsigned int index (bounded and unbounded variants)
workload: Chapter02 01/03/04_substring_sort.C: std::sort of 2^14 pointers into a 2^18-character string (mostly 'a', one random letter per 1024 chars) with a lambda calling compare() in a separate translation unit; wall time of the sort by std::chrono::system_clock, single run.
claimed_speedup: Book: unsigned bounded compare 98 ms, unsigned without the bound check 210 ms, signed int index 74 ms for the same sort, so the signed version is about 1.3x faster than the bounded unsigned one and about 2.8x faster than the unbounded unsigned one (both derived from the book figures).
compiler_and_flags: $CXX (GCC or Clang, unspecified) with -g -O3 --std=c++17 per the build comments in the Chapter02 sources
tradeoffs: Relies on signed overflow being undefined so the compiler can assume the index never wraps; strings or loops past INT_MAX characters would be undefined behaviour. Chapter11 (04a_compare1.C and 04b_compare2.C) repeats the idea with no numbers in the text.
caveats: The timing numbers are the book's own (quoted in the seed lead); the repository carries the benchmark program but no results file, so the numbers do not appear on the benchmark_url page and the ratios could not be checked against it. Compiler is only 'GCC or Clang'. Baseline is a hand-written byte loop, not std::memcmp or std::strcmp, which would probably beat all three variants and was not tried. It is odd that the unbounded unsigned loop (210 ms) is slower than the bounded one (98 ms); the explanation is compiler-specific code generation, so another compiler or version may show a different ordering. Single timed run with a deterministic minstd_rand seed; the data are almost constant, so many comparisons run to the end of a long equal prefix.

baseline: Per-thread counters stored adjacent in a plain unsigned long array (false sharing)
workload: Chapter05/04_local_incr.C (Google Benchmark, 1 to numcpu threads, real time): each thread increments its own counter 1024 times per iteration then adds it to a global atomic; BM_false_shared uses x2a[thread_index], BM_not_shared uses x3a[16*thread_index] (128-byte stride).

name: The Art of Writing Efficient Programs: std::atomic counter increment instead of a mutex-guarded counter
workload: Chapter06/01a_atomic_count.C against 01b_mutex_count.C (and BM_atomic against BM_mutex in 01_sharing_incr_mbm.C): Google Benchmark, one shared counter incremented by 1 to numcpu threads, real time.
claimed_speedup: Book: single-thread increment costs 23 ns under a mutex versus 7 ns for the atomic (about 3.3x, derived from the book figures); the gap widens with more threads.
tradeoffs: Atomic fetch_add only guards a single word; anything bigger than one counter needs a lock or a lock-free design.
caveats: The timing numbers are the book's own (quoted in the seed lead); the repository carries the benchmark program but no results file, so the numbers do not appear on the benchmark_url page and the ratios could not be checked against it. Obvious result for a one-word counter; the interest is the size of the gap. In 01_sharing_incr_mbm.C BM_atomic repeats the increment 64 times per iteration but reports 32 items per iteration, which doubles its reported time per item, so the per-item figures from that file are inconsistent; 01a_atomic_count.C does one fetch_add per iteration and is correct. Chapter05/03_mutex_incr.C has the opposite mistake (32 lock and increment per iteration, 1024 items reported). Compiler, flags, CPU and standard library not stated, and the cost of an uncontended std::mutex differs between libstdc++, libc++ and MSVC.

name: The Art of Writing Efficient Programs: publishing pointer (ts_unique_ptr) instead of an atomic std::shared_ptr
baseline: std::shared_ptr accessed through std::atomic_load_explicit and std::atomic_store_explicit
workload: Chapter06/03_owning_ptr_mbm.C against 03b_shared_ptr_mbm.C and 03a_raw_ptr_mbm.C (Google Benchmark, 1 to numcpu consumer threads, real time): BM_ptr_deref of a published object and BM_ptr_assign of a new pointer; ts_unique_ptr is a std::atomic<T*> with release publish and acquire get.
claimed_speedup: Book: single-threaded dereference matches a raw pointer and std::unique_ptr, and the publishing pointer is about 60 times faster than the atomic std::shared_ptr on one thread (Figures 6.5 to 6.7 hold the chart).
tradeoffs: Not a drop-in replacement: get() returns a raw pointer, there is no shared ownership, publish() does not free the object it replaces (the benchmark just republishes one pointer), so retired objects must be kept alive or reclaimed by the caller, and readers can dangle if a writer deletes. Single writer and many readers is the intended use.
caveats: The timing numbers are the book's own (quoted in the seed lead); the repository carries the benchmark program but no results file, so the numbers do not appear on the benchmark_url page and the ratios could not be checked against it. The 60x is mostly the cost of the library's atomic shared_ptr access: libstdc++ and libc++ have implemented std::atomic_load on a shared_ptr through a global mutex pool, so the ratio depends on the standard library and version (C++20 std::atomic<std::shared_ptr> differs again) and the book does not name it. Compiler, flags and CPU not stated. The baseline does extra work (reference counting) that the publishing pointer avoids by design, so it is a different safety contract and not a like-for-like swap.

name: The Art of Writing Efficient Programs: spinlock-guarded thread-safe stack
workload: Chapter07/02_stack.C (Google Benchmark, 1 to numcpu threads, real time): BM_stack (mt_stack with the test-and-test-and-set spinlock from spinlock.h) against BM_stack1 (mt_stack1 with std::mutex); each iteration pushes then pops one int. Chapter07/03_queue.C has the same pairing for a queue.
claimed_speedup: Book: spinlock stack about 70 million operations per second against about 30 million for the mutex stack on one thread (about 2.3x, derived from the book figures; Figures 7.3 and 7.11); an unlocked std::stack reaches about 485 million on the same machine.
hardware: x86 machine for the 70M and 30M figures; CPU model not stated
tradeoffs: The spinlock backs off with a 1 ns nanosleep after 8 failed spins; on a loaded or oversubscribed machine, or with a preempted lock holder, spinning wastes cores and can invert priorities. Not fair, not recursive, no condition-variable integration.
caveats: The timing numbers are the book's own (quoted in the seed lead); the repository carries the benchmark program but no results file, so the numbers do not appear on the benchmark_url page and the ratios could not be checked against it. The single-thread comparison measures uncontended lock cost, not behaviour under contention; the book's own multi-thread charts are image-only. The same chapter says the lock-free stack does not beat the spinlock stack on x86. BM_stack0 (unlocked reference) is not registered in the file. Compiler, flags and CPU not stated; std::mutex cost varies by standard library.

name: The Art of Writing Efficient Programs: preallocate-once buffer instead of new[] and delete[] every iteration
baseline: Per-iteration new char[N] / delete[] (system operator new)
workload: Chapter09/04_buffer.C (Google Benchmark, 1 to numcpu threads, real time): build a random-size string of up to 1 KB with memset; BM_make_str_new allocates and frees each iteration, BM_make_str_max reuses one buffer of the maximum size allocated before the loop, BM_make_str_buf uses a grow-only buffer.
claimed_speedup: Book: allocating every iteration runs at about 40% of the speed of the version that allocates the maximum size once (preallocation about 2.5x faster, derived from the book figure); the penalty is larger with 8 threads (charts only).
tradeoffs: Holds the maximum buffer for the object's lifetime and needs the maximum size known or bounded; shared across calls it is not thread-safe unless one buffer per thread.
caveats: The timing numbers are the book's own (quoted in the seed lead); the repository carries the benchmark program but no results file, so the numbers do not appear on the benchmark_url page and the ratios could not be checked against it. Hoisting an allocation out of a loop is a general idiom, and the size of the win depends on the allocator (glibc malloc, tcmalloc and jemalloc differ) which the book does not name. The harness fills its random-size table with v[i] = rand() after only reserve(), writing past size() (undefined behaviour, works in practice), and the baseline also pays memset and a never-taken cout branch that the compared variants share. Compiler, flags and CPU not stated.
